content:
Long-term arthritis pain can affect sleep, mood and independence. When usual treatments are not enough, a pain clinic may help.

This guide explains what pain clinics offer. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

What a pain clinic may offer

  • A review of pain medicines.
  • Physiotherapy and activity planning.
  • Psychological support, such as CBT or acceptance and commitment therapy.
  • Pain management programmes.
  • Some injections.

Medicines in frailty

Older people can be more sensitive to side effects such as drowsiness, confusion and constipation. NICE guidance on chronic pain advises caution with some medicines, including opioids. Do not stop medicines without advice.

Referral

Ask your GP or hospital team about referral. Waiting times vary.

Preparing

  • Keep a pain diary.
  • List your medicines.
  • Think about your goals.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will they get rid of my pain?

The aim is often to reduce pain and improve how you live with it.

Can they visit at home?

Usually not, but some services offer phone or video appointments.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s

If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
